Upward-leaning: Senate Commerce (30 July) punted its broader AI markup to after summer recess, with the Thune/Cruz/Klobuchar advanced-AI bill on hold amid disagreements with Anthropic and Cantwell — formal statutory pacing is now less imminent, marginally preserving lab discretion. forecasts.base_rate: Reference class: publicly announced technology-milestone declarations by major labs within a fixed ~3.5-year window, conditioned on current frontier progress. On the downside-pressure ledger: TechCrunch's running list (25 July) added Monday.com as the ~21st company citing AI in 2026 layoffs, and YTD trackers through 26 July show ~170,500 tech-sector cuts with IT services/consulting the second-largest category (~31,900) — consistent with the already-priced McKinsey 3,000-4,000 cut and Accenture's ~11,000-role restructuring. forecasts.base_rate: Historical base rate of an established professional-services sector losing ≥33% of revenue or employment within ~6 years of a technology shock is very low (<10%); even disrupted sectors (e.g., legal process, travel agencies pre-internet took longer) rarely compress that fast. Adjusted upward for unusually direct AI substitution of core consulting tasks and visible 2025-26 cuts: ~15-25% range.

forecasts.question: Will UK annual CPI inflation fall below 2.0% for at least one month before 1 January 2027?
forecasts.key_change: Lower (effectively 1% -> ~0.5%, recorded as 1 with tightened CI 0-2). A DOWN trigger fired: the MPC held Bank Rate at 3.75% on 30 July but by 6-3, with Greene, Mann and Pill voting for a hike to 4.00% — the third consecutive meeting with a growing hawkish minority (8-1 April, 7-2 June, 6-3 July), signalling the Bank sees upside, not downside, inflation risk. The new Monetary Policy Report projects CPI peaking around 3.2% in 2026 Q4 (pessimistic Middle East scenario: up to 4.5% in 2027), confirming a rising path through every remaining print publishable before 1 Jan 2027. Bailey noted inflation had 'fallen faster than we'd expected' but said Middle East energy costs 'will cause inflation to rise again later this year.' Oil partially retraced but stayed high: Brent briefly topped $93 after renewed US-Iran strikes, then eased to ~$88 on 31 July as Hormuz crude flows showed recovery — well above the sub-$75 level needed to change the picture. June CPI was 2.6%, the 13% Ofgem cap rise hits July's print, and analyst consensus sees ~3.5% by Q4. A sub-2.0% print now requires a ~0.7pp+ collapse against a projected ~0.6pp rise within five publishable months — close to a measurement-error-only scenario.
forecasts.base_rate: Historically, UK CPI has fallen 0.7pp+ within 5 months against a central-bank-projected rise in fewer than ~5% of comparable episodes, and essentially only during abrupt energy price collapses (2014-15, 2020); with an active oil-supply shock pushing the other way, the applicable base rate is ~1-2%.

factors_up.factor: Bailey conceded inflation had fallen faster than the Bank expected pre-conflict; June CPI at 2.6% beat forecasts
Hormuz crude flows recovering; Brent eased from $93+ to ~$88, and Cornwall Insight sees the October Ofgem cap possibly lower than July's
Government direct interventions could be visibly disinflationary for measured CPI from late 2026

13% July Ofgem price cap rise (gas +24%) mechanically lifts July-September CPI prints
Brent ~$88 after US-Iran strikes, still far above pre-conflict levels; sticky services inflation keeps the hike risk live

forecasts.question: Will UK average annual real GDP growth exceed 1.5% across the 2030s (2030-2039)?
forecasts.key_change: Hold at 34% (CI 21-48). The pending mover has now landed: the BoE's July MPR and decision (published 12pm, 30 July) held Bank Rate at 3.75% on a 6-3 vote, with dissent widening from two to three — Greene, Mann and Pill wanted a hike to 4.0%. Crucially for this question, the MPR contained no supply-side upgrade: staff potential supply growth estimates remain around 0.3-0.4% per quarter (~1.2-1.6% annualised, straddling but not clearly above the 1.5% threshold), and the projection shows GDP growth of just 1.1% in Q3 2026 and Q3 2027 — the energy shock keeps the economy 'subdued' through early 2027 — recovering to 1.7% by Q3 2028 as the drag fades. CPI is seen peaking at 3.2% in Q4 2026 then undershooting to 1.7% in Q1 2028. Neither update trigger fired: no productivity revision above 1.25%, and 2026-27 projections (1.1%) sit above the sub-1% DOWN trigger. Market reaction was benign — 2y gilts rallied 11bp to 4.34%, 10y steady at 5.04%, below the 5.25% trigger; 30y ~5.75% after Burnham's fiscal-flexibility episode. Mildly softer near-term growth offsets the reassuring 2028 pickup; net neutral, so no change.
forecasts.base_rate: ~35-40%: for mature advanced economies in the post-2008 low-productivity regime, roughly a third of rolling decades achieve average real GDP growth above 1.5%; UK 2010s averaged ~1.8% but 2020s are tracking ~1%, and BoE/OECD trend estimates (~1.0-1.4%) sit below the threshold.

Recent momentum: GDP grew 0.7% in three months to May, G7-leading and roughly double BoE trend pace
Inflation projected to undershoot target (1.7% Q1 2028), implying room for rate cuts supporting activity into the late 2020s
HMT-compiled consensus for 2026 growth nudged up to 1.0% from 0.9%
Possible AI-driven productivity acceleration in the 2030s not embedded in official trend estimates

factors_down.factor: BoE potential supply growth still only ~0.3-0.4% per quarter (~1.2-1.6% annualised); no supply-side upgrade in July MPR; OECD trend ~1%
MPR projects subdued growth of 1.1% in both 2026 and 2027 on the energy shock — weak jumping-off point for the 2030s
Elevated gilt yields (10y ~5.04%, 30y ~5.75%, highest in G7) raise debt-service costs and crowd out growth-enhancing investment
Hawkish MPC drift (dissent widened to 3 for a hike; Pill signalling rates may need to rise) keeps policy tighter for longer
Fiscal credibility strain after PM Burnham's 'fiscal flexibility' remarks; risk of consolidation squeezing capital budgets
Structural headwinds: ageing demographics, weak business investment, persistent post-2008 productivity stagnation

key_uncertainties: Whether AI/technology diffusion lifts UK productivity growth materially above the ~1% post-2008 trend during the 2030s
Duration and depth of the Middle East energy shock and its scarring effects on investment
OBR Autumn 2026 productivity assumptions and whether Burnham government fiscal choices preserve capital spending
Whether elevated gilt yields (highest in G7) persist, raising the cost of capital through the late 2020s
Delivery of housing/infrastructure programmes and planning reform at scale by 2028-2030
Labour supply trajectory: migration policy, inactivity and participation trends into the 2030s
update_triggers: UP if BoE MPR or OBR revise trend productivity growth above 1.25%, or annual growth exceeds 2% in consecutive years
UP if large-scale housing/infrastructure delivery visibly on track by 2028
DOWN if OBR downgrades productivity assumptions in Autumn 2026, or 2026-27 growth outturns undershoot 1% (MPR now projects 1.1% both years — close to trigger)
DOWN if 10y gilt yields sustained above ~5.25% (currently ~5.04% post-MPC)
DOWN if MPC pivots to actual hikes (watch 17 September meeting; hawkish dissent now 3 of 9)
